title: Ilford Boy - theatre review
transcript: Hello, welcome to Theatre Reviews with Paul 7. I'm here at the Donmar Warehouse to see Ilford Boy. It's said that conflict is an essential building brick of a good story. Well, if that's true, you could build a house with this play. You've got three sisters who are jealous and even contemptuous of each other, uh but of course love each other as well. Um and then each sister has a tempestuous relationship with their partner. Um and those partners, being straight men in the 1990s, are in various degrees of conflict with a gay friend of the family. Um and there's a teenage boy in conflict with his father and himself over being gay. Keep watching and I'll give you more details about just how funny all this is, even as sad truths about their relationships seep through the comedy. But first, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel and visit my website, theatre.reviews, where you can read my reviews and my roundups of other critics' reviews, including of Ilford Boy. The story, set in Ilford, East London, flits back and forth between 1980 and 1995. And incidentally, the play is almost worth seeing just for the nostalgia, such is the detail and accuracy of references to the period. Now in 1980, the sisters are strappy teenagers, and their mum is the benign matriarch. In 1995, mum, now known as Nan, has died. And the girls are all married. And the oldest, Tilly, has a teenage son, Ted. So part of what Donny Lee is bringing us in his play is not only the difficulty of being gay back then, but also how behaviour and attitudes repeat through the generations, unless someone chooses to break the chain. The sisters influenced by their mother are, on the whole, tolerant and caring. Tilly, an outstanding performance from Ria Zmitrovich, uh that throbs with life, cannot fully break free from her abusive partner Ken. Anne, played by Charlotte Jackeley, is loud and vulnerable and in a coercive relationship with husband Raj. Jackie, played by Jodie McNee, seems to have her husband, Trevor, under her thumb. The women dominate the play as they so often dominate working-class families, and the actors playing them are outstanding, um emotions exploding like fireworks on Bonfire Night and shooting out one-liners with exquisite timing. Uh my favorite being, you can't turn a dog into a chair, and if you do, it won't be comfy. All their relationships have sad secrets which are revealed in the course of the play. The men are all messed up. Find me a play these days when they aren't. Um Ken, a boxer, was beaten by his father and saw his mother physically abused, and much as he may try to be a better husband and a more sensitive father, he still seeks to prove his manhood through violence, philandering, and an acquired homophobia against his gay friend. His relationship with his son Ted is is subtle. Um the boy tries to ingratiate himself with his dad by taking up boxing and says the bullying he's receiving at school is about his mixed race, uh which he thinks his black father might sympathise with, uh, rather than the truth, uh, which is that he's being picked on for being gay. As an aside, it's interesting that race gets hardly a mention, uh, in in a play that mixes white, brown and black working-class characters. Ken is torn between wanting his son to take after him and wanting his son to be himself. It's a convincingly anguished performance from, uh, Gershwin Eustace Jr. Aaron Gill invests Raj with a skin crawling creepiness as he quietly but firmly controls his wife. Kerry Crankson as the sad-eyed guileless Trevor slowly reveals the heartache behind his accession to Jackie's, uh, henpecking. And there's Patrick the Pouf, as he continues to be known within the family from his school days to the present. He's given a moving portrayal by Craig Stein. As a gay black man, he presents Ted with a role model both in how a gay man can expect to be treated and how to rise above it. Patrick presents a confident face but hides his heartbreak at his ostracism and the scourge of AIDS. He also provides the standout moment of the entire evening when, at the encouragement of Ted, he dances to Don't Rain on My Parade. So much joy is released as neon lights come on and he taps and jumps on and off the coffee table and all around the stage inches from the noses of the audience. And this is a high point of a motif running through the play, namely the importance of theatre as an art form based on empathy. Characters gay and straight alike love the Torch songs and their singers, like Barbara Strassand, that put them in touch with their own and others' feelings, and specifically enable the gay characters to see their life in a positive way. And the choice of Don't Rain on My Parade, a song about being yourself and pursuing your dreams, is not an accident. Ted is further inspired by seeing a black man as a lead in a musical. And in a wonderful meta moment, it's Adrian Lester in Company, which actually played at the Donmar back in 1996. You're watching Theatre Reviews with Paul Seven. I've been reviewing on YouTube now for over nine years, so thank you for joining me. And please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. And also, you can read my reviews and my Theatre Review roundups at theatre.reviews. Keep watching for more about Ilford Boy. Being the Donmar, the play, this play, is performed with the audience on three sides, so you're you're right there with the family as they joke and bicker. And there's a visceral fight scene in Act two which made me jump in my seat. The most striking element of the set, designed by Peter Mackintosh, is that you can see through to a staircase and upper landing at the back, giving characters somewhere to escape to while still in view. The set leaves plenty of room for the actors to move around, and they are beautifully choreographed by director Tim Sheader. There's some seating and tables. A coffee table in the first act, a dining table in the second. Unfortunately, despite all the humor and anguish, Danny Winter doesn't bring much that's new to the table. Uh, the characters and the trials of coming out as gay are familiar stereotypes from the play's many theatrical and screen predecessors. Billy Elliot springs to mind, but also It's a Sin, Fun Home, Everybody's Talking About Jamie, and many more. The characters are interesting and the acting is superb. The dialogue is funny, but there is a lack of depth. Still, even if it has the substance of a soufflé, like a soufflé, it's delicious while it lasts. And I give It 's a Boy four stars. I hope you found this review interesting and useful. And if you did, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel, then you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. Uh, you can also visit my website, theatre.reviews, to read my reviews and uh my roundups of other critics' reviews. And you can follow me on various social media like Instagram, Mastodon, um Threads, and uh BlueSky. Happy theatre going.
